paragraphs.heading: Who Newton was
paragraphs.text: Isaac Newton was an English thinker of many talents who lived from 1643 to 1727. He was a mathematician, physicist and astronomer, but also an alchemist, a theologian, a historian and an inventor. He stands as a central figure of the Scientific Revolution and of the Enlightenment that came after it. His work is seen as the most influential of all in bringing about modern science.

paragraphs.heading: One set of laws for everything
paragraphs.text: In 1687 Newton first published his Principia, short for Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. The book established classical mechanics and achieved the first great unification in physics. In it he set out his laws of motion and of universal gravitation, and he showed that objects on Earth and bodies in the sky obey the very same principles. His laws stayed the leading scientific view for centuries, until the theory of relativity replaced them. They still work well enough whenever speeds are far below the speed of light and gravity is weak.

paragraphs.heading: Gravity explains the sky
paragraphs.text: Using his mathematical account of gravity, Newton derived Kepler's laws of how planets move. He also explained the tides, the paths of comets and the precession of the equinoxes, and this removed doubt that the planets circle the Sun. He reasoned that Earth is an oblate spheroid. Later measurements of Earth's shape by Maupertuis, Clairaut, La Condamine and others confirmed this, and that convinced most European scientists that his mechanics beat the older systems.

paragraphs.heading: Light, colour and calculus
paragraphs.text: Newton built the first reflecting telescope. He also developed a detailed theory of colour, starting from the fact that a prism splits white light into the colours of the visible spectrum, and gathered his work on light in the book Opticks in 1704. In 1665 he found the generalised binomial theorem and started on the mathematics that later became calculus. He shares the credit for calculus with the German mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, though Newton worked it out years before him.

paragraphs.heading: Early life
paragraphs.text: Newton was born at Woolsthorpe Manor, in a Lincolnshire hamlet, on Christmas Day 1642 by the calendar England used then. His father, also called Isaac, had died three months earlier. He arrived early and was so tiny that his mother said he could have fitted in a quart mug. When he was three she remarried and moved in with her new husband, leaving the boy with his grandmother. In June 1661 he entered Trinity College, Cambridge.

paragraphs.heading: Mint, Parliament and the Royal Society
paragraphs.text: At 26 Newton became the second Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge. He twice sat briefly in Parliament for the university. Queen Anne knighted him in 1705, and he spent his last thirty years in London running the Royal Mint, where he made British coins more accurate and more secure. He led the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727, died at 84, and became the first scientist buried in Westminster Abbey.
